item.content:encoded:
AI CLI Tools Community Digest 2026-11-27

Generated: 2026-11-26 17:29 UTC | Tools covered: 2

  • Claude Code
  • OpenCode
  • Claude Code Skills

Cross-Tool Comparison

AI CLI Tools Cross-Comparison Report — 2026-11-27

Only two tools, Claude Code and OpenCode, are covered in today's digests. The comparison is limited to them. Counts come from the digests. Where a digest gave no number, I say so.

1. Ecosystem Overview

Both communities are working through the cost of growth. Their extension surfaces are expanding (Claude Code Mods, OpenCode v2 subagents and agent widgets). Agent autonomy is also producing safety and reliability problems. Windows quality, runaway or unrequested agent behavior, and opaque usage limits show up in both. The tools differ in model. Claude Code is a closed-source, first-party product, and its open-source PRs (#41518, #41447) are unofficial. OpenCode is open-source and multi-provider, with its own paid tier (OpenCode Go).

2. Activity Comparison

Metric Claude Code OpenCode
Hot issues listed 10 10
Top issue by comments #60705 (324, closed) #59387 (411, open)
PRs updated (24h) 3 At least 10 listed (digest gives no total)
Release status None v2.4.2
Release content n/a GPT-6.2 system prompt, OpenCode Go onboarding fix (notes truncated)

Caveat: the listed hot issues are a sample, not a full count of issues opened or updated. The PR comparison is not like for like, since Claude Code's figure is a total and OpenCode's is a lower bound.

3. Shared Feature Directions

Need Claude Code OpenCode
Extensibility and agent orchestration Mods and hooks (#91870, 👍 132) Subagent control: foreground mode (#64073), cancellation (#36423), agent widgets (PR #65261)
Session management Project-local memory (#25947), --continue/--resume registry (#69364), nested session groups (#93058) Auto-resume toggle (#56032), V1→V2 session visibility (#49827), cross-session questions (PR #60074)
Usage and quota transparency Usage and limit anomalies (#112473, #111593), /usage breakage (#71886) Quota warnings (#42765), free-tier exhaustion (#59387)
Windows reliability Backslash halving (#85856), 8 KB truncation (#85111), flashing consoles (#66540) Flashing consoles (#52266), destructive rd /s /q quoting (#66449)
Better model and tool behavior Instruction-following (#60705, #69044) Loop protection (#45442), model-specific prompts (GPT-6.2 in PR #66297, Kimi prompt change in PR #66538)

4. Differentiation Analysis

  • Claude Code: Users are heavy daily users. Their feedback centers on model instruction-following, tool correctness (silent content mutation in #72957, filename guards in #44657), and desktop app UX. The strongest request is Mods and hook extensibility. The most-upvoted request is a terminal rendering flag (#43113, 👍 73). Process work is visible (stale-bot change, PR #112436).
  • OpenCode: The v2 architecture is mid-transition. Feedback focuses on subagent semantics, migration regressions, and provider or billing issues. It is multi-provider, so it deals with provider quirks (Copilot GPT-6 cache loss in #59868, gateway context-overflow handling in PR #66623). It also runs a free tier and OpenCode Go, so billing and regional payment problems (#52958) affect it directly. Its MCP and OAuth fixes (PR #66636, 11 issues) point to enterprise and integration use.
  • Target users: Claude Code serves users inside one vendor's ecosystem who want depth. OpenCode serves users who want provider choice and an open stack.

5. Community Momentum & Maturity

  • Claude Code: Engagement is high but concentrated in older threads. The top threads have 281, 324 and 146 comments. There was no release and little PR activity (3 PRs) in the window. This reads as a mature, stable product whose community focuses on feedback and process, not fast iteration.
  • OpenCode: It iterates faster. It shipped a release and has many fresh PRs. Several regressions were fixed quickly (#66389, #66637). Its largest thread (#59387, 411 comments) is an unresolved free-tier problem. It is evolving quickly, but with migration debt.

I did not measure momentum beyond one day of data, so treat these as a snapshot.

6. Trend Signals

  1. Agent safety is now a product requirement. Examples are the drive-root deletion (#66449), directives taken as authorization (#60705), and runaway loops (#45442). Developers should expect sandboxing, loop limits and confirmation gates to become differentiators.
  2. Subagents are the contested interface. OpenCode users want blocking and cancellable subagents. Background-only execution is not accepted without control.
  3. Cost transparency is a growing complaint. Both communities report limits that are unclear or behave unexpectedly. Claude Code's usage reports are unconfirmed and could be a metering bug, so verify before drawing conclusions.
  4. Windows remains a weak platform for both tools. Teams on Windows should plan for extra testing, and WSL may be the safer route.
  5. Per-model prompt tuning is spreading. OpenCode's GPT-6.2 prompt shows that multi-provider tools now maintain model-specific behavior.

Recommendation: Choose Claude Code for a polished single-vendor experience, and accept slower public iteration. Choose OpenCode for provider flexibility, and expect v2 migration friction. For either tool, restrict destructive shell permissions on Windows and monitor usage independently.

Per-Tool Reports

Claude Code — anthropics/claude-code

Claude Code Skills Highlights

Source: anthropics/skills

Claude Code Skills Community Highlights (data as of 2026-11-27)

Data caveat: The PR feed returned Comments: undefined and 0 👍 for every PR, so the PR ranking below follows the feed's order and my read of each PR's relevance. It is not a verified comment count. Issue comment counts are real. All 20 PRs are still OPEN, and none has merged.

1. Top Skills Ranking (PRs)

# Skill / PR What it does Highlights Status
1 #1742 mcp-builder fix Supports mcp>=2 (streamable_http_client rename, custom headers via create_mcp_http_client) Fixes #1668. It is a breaking-API compatibility fix, and mcp-builder is broken for new installs without it. Open (updated 2026-10-08)
2 #1298 skill-creator trigger evals Isolates trigger evals and handles Windows select() failures and runtime errors It targets false-miss and invalid-score bugs in the eval loop. This matches the open issues #556 and #1352. Open (updated 2026-09-16)
3 #1980 webapp-testing Removes shell=True from with_server.py (CWE-78 command injection) A security hardening fix. Open (updated 2026-11-01)
4 #1792 docx accept_changes.py now reports LibreOffice timeouts as errors and verifies that no revision marks remain It fixes a silent-success bug. Open (updated 2026-11-01)
5 #2019 xlsx Resolves worksheet-scoped defined names and aliases in external_links_at_risk Fixes #2013. It removes false negatives in external-link detection. Open (updated 2026-11-03)
6 #1245 New skills Adds notion-spec-to-implementation and quantitative-resume-auditor A new-skill submission that turns Notion specs into implementable tasks. It has been open since June. Open (updated 2026-10-15)
7 #525 pyxel Retro game development skill with headless input-driven runs and frame inspection One of the oldest open PRs (March). It is still being updated. Open (updated 2026-11-01)
8 #1681 skill-creator Makes package_skill.py runnable directly and updates usage paths Fixes a ModuleNotFoundError on direct execution. Open (updated 2026-11-19)

2. Community Demand Trends (from Issues)

  1. Reliable skill evaluation and triggering. #556 (13 comments) reports a 0% trigger rate in run_eval.py. #1352 reports parallel workers cross-matching skill UUIDs and giving false-negative rates. #2064 says the theme-factory description says what the skill does but not when to use it.
  2. Trust, security and provenance. #492 (46 comments, the most active issue) covers community skills being distributed under the anthropic/ namespace. This is also the theme of the shell=True fix in PR #1980.
  3. Context and token efficiency. #1487 reports claude-api eagerly injecting about 156k tokens. #189 reports duplicate skills from the document-skills and example-skills plugins. #202 asks that skill-creator follow best practice.
  4. Agent memory, governance and quality gates. #1329 proposes compact-memory. #1385 proposes a Reasoning Quality Gate Pipeline. #412 proposed agent-governance and is closed.
  5. Document-skill correctness. #2018 reports docx merge_runs.py writing invalid XML. #1868 reports a gradient off-by-one in slack-gif-creator.
  6. Sharing and distribution. #228 asks for org-wide skill sharing in Claude.ai.

#1143 (account email change, 20 👍) and #62 (skills disappeared) are platform or account issues, not skill requests.

3. High-Potential Pending Skills

These are small, well-scoped bug fixes with a clear linked issue, so they are the most likely to merge:

  • #1742: mcp-builder mcp>=2 compatibility. It blocks current users.
  • #1298, plus #1997 (YAML frontmatter parsing) and #1681: skill-creator and eval fixes. They address the most-discussed bug cluster (#556, #1352).
  • #1980: the webapp-testing security fix.
  • #1792 and #2019: docx and xlsx correctness fixes.
  • #1950: updates the claude-api pause_turn guidance for Python SDK 1.1.0.
  • #1975, #1976 and #1977: trivial one-line fixes, each linked to an issue.

New-skill PRs (#1245, #525, #514, #1703, #1771, #1615) have waited months with no merge signal, so I'd rate them lower. This repo mostly accepts fixes to existing skills, not community additions.

4. Skills Ecosystem Insight

The community's demand is concentrated on making existing official skills trustworthy and reliable: working evals and triggering, security hardening, and correct document-skill tooling. New skill submissions are secondary and mostly stalled.

Claude Code Community Digest — 2026-11-27

1. Today's Highlights

No new releases shipped in the last 24h. Activity centers on long-running threads: the Mods extensibility initiative (#91870) and model-behavior feedback (#60705, #69044). New usage and limit anomaly reports (#112473, #111593) and a PR to stop auto-staling reproducible issues (#112436) also stand out.

2. Releases

None in the last 24h.

3. Hot Issues

  1. #91870 Mods – make Claude 10x more extensible [OPEN, 281 comments, 👍 132]. This is the most-endorsed item. The author reports Mods are now live (Oct 1 update) and says feedback is being worked through. It signals a major push on hooks and plugins as the extension surface.

  2. #60705 /goal Stop-hook directive cited as authorization for unrequested actions [CLOSED, 324 comments]. This is the most-discussed thread. It documents model-side behaviors that user CLAUDE.md rules didn't catch: treating a hook directive as authorization, treating absence from search as evidence of absence, and caving under pushback.

  3. #69044 Recurring errors documented over months of daily use [OPEN, 146 comments]. A structured long-term feedback document from a daily user. It reflects broader concern about model reliability and instruction-following.

  4. #86142 MCP servers declaring draft-07 outputSchema rejected as "unsupported dialect" [CLOSED, 57 comments, 👍 14]. It blocked MCP servers client-side before dispatch. It's now closed, which is relevant to MCP server authors.

  5. #85856 Windows/Git Bash halves backslashes in Bash tool commands [OPEN, 👍 24]. A command-line encoding mismatch between MSVCRT and MSYS2 silently corrupts commands, and quoting can't work around it. It's a serious correctness bug for Windows users.

  6. #85111 Bash tool silently truncates commands over ~8 KB on Windows [OPEN, 👍 12]. The truncation is reported as a quoting error, which misleads users. It's another Windows tool-reliability issue.

  7. #72957 Write/Edit tools decode \uXXXX in file content [OPEN, reproduced]. Literal escape sequences can't be stored in files, which corrupts content. It affects anyone writing source or config files containing escapes.

  8. #44657 Subagent Write rejects .md files named report/summary/findings/analysis [OPEN, 👍 35]. A hard-coded filename guard with no opt-out blocks legitimate agent workflows.

  9. #112473 Abnormally high usage consumption despite short outputs and #111593 Weekly limit jumped 30% → 88% in 13.5h. Both are fresh, both are tagged cost, and they are the first reports of usage-accounting concerns in this window. Together they suggest a possible metering regression, but the reports are unconfirmed.

  10. #74023 settings.json resolves against literal cwd, not git root [CLOSED, reproduced]. Launching from a subdirectory silently dropped all project settings. It's now closed and documented.

4. Key PR Progress

Only 3 PRs were updated in the last 24h:

  1. #112436 Don't mark reproducible or high-impact issues as stale. The stale sweep will skip issues labeled has repro, reproduced, data-loss, or high-priority. This is a maintainer-process improvement and responds to real bugs getting auto-closed.
  2. #41518 Fully Open Source Claude Code. A community PR that reconstructs the source from the npm cli.js.map and adds a Bun build. It's unofficial and has legal and provenance implications.
  3. #41447 feat: open source claude code. A similar community PR that references several long-standing issues. It's also unofficial.

There are no further notable PRs in the window.

5. Feature Request Trends

  • Extensibility and hooks. Mods (#91870) is the dominant theme.
  • Desktop UX. Auto-expanding diffs (#61280), nested session groups (#93058), and pinning Routine runs in the sidebar (#54517).
  • Session and memory management. Project-local memory in .claude/memory (#25947), and a live-session registry check for --continue/--resume (#69364).
  • Terminal rendering. A flag to emit long lines and let the terminal wrap (#43113, 👍 73, the most-upvoted request here).
  • Voice. Hands-free voice conversation mode (#111520).

6. Developer Pain Points

  • Windows reliability. Backslash halving, 8 KB truncation, flashing console windows (#66540), IME overlap (#70955), and MSIX launch failures (#98328).
  • Model instruction-following. Ignored orders, unrequested changes to procedures and memory (#97182, #99180), and the patterns in #60705 and #69044.
  • Usage and limit opacity. Unexplained consumption jumps (#112473, #111593), and DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC silently breaking /usage (#71886).
  • Tool surprises. Silent content mutation (#72957) and hidden filename restrictions (#44657).
  • Desktop trust and privacy. Unrequested background git fetch with no off switch (#84698), and auto-mode refusals caused by the app rewriting inputs (#108921).
  • Session and settings correctness. /rename affecting concurrent sessions (#86531), and Linux desktop no_new_privs regressing so Snap browser links don't open (#102029).
OpenCode — anomalyco/opencode

OpenCode Community Digest — 2026-11-27

1. Today's Highlights

OpenCode v2.4.2 ships a GPT-6.2-specific system prompt (for gpt-latest aliases) and an OpenCode Go onboarding fix. The community is still focused on v2 migration gaps: subagent behavior (foreground vs. always-background, cancellation, loop protection), session/project handling after V1→V2 upgrade, and free-tier quota problems. A Windows data-loss report (rd /s /q wiping a drive root) is the most serious safety issue in the data.

2. Releases

v2.4.2 (the notes were truncated, so details are limited)

  • GPT-6.2 system prompt: GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra, plus the gpt-latest aliases, now use a prompt written for GPT-6.2 (#66297).
  • OpenCode Go onboarding fix: After you connect OpenCode, the model picker lists OpenCode Go first. The rest of this item was cut off.

3. Hot Issues

  1. #59387 Free tier issues megathread (411 comments, 31 👍). It collects "Free usage exceeded" errors and resets that never happen. It is the largest source of user friction.
  2. #64073 Restore foreground subagent execution (36 comments, 13 👍). Users want blocking subagent calls back.
  3. #64096 Keep a blocking subagent option (9 comments). It is the same concern as #64073, aimed at the always-background change in 2.3.0.
  4. #66449 Windows bash tool rd /s /q deleted a drive root (closed, 7 comments). A model-generated command with escaped quotes resolved to \, the drive root. The report cites about 270k files lost. This is a critical safety and quoting bug.
  5. #52958 OpenCode Go payments declined from Italy/EU (32 comments). Subscriptions fail across several payment methods, which blocks revenue and adoption.
  6. #49827 V1→V2 migration hides non-git "global" sessions (24 comments). Users lose access to their history in the session picker.
  7. #36423 No cancellation for background subagents (19 comments, 10 👍). There is no way to stop a running subagent.
  8. #45442 Subagent loop: 364 identical grep calls over ~50 minutes (12 comments). There is no loop protection, so tokens burn without control.
  9. #66389 v1→v2 migration marks client tools executed: true, wedging OpenAI Chat sessions on 2.3.2 (closed, 7 comments). It was a quickly handled regression.
  10. #52266 Windows: console windows flash for every spawned process (13 comments, 8 👍). CREATE_NO_WINDOW is not set, and the report says this is a recurring problem.

4. Key PR Progress

  1. #66636: Fixes a batch of MCP OAuth, connection and prompt issues. It closes 11 issues.
  2. #66641: Mirrors TUI copies through Windows interop on WSL, so the "Copied" message matches what actually reaches the clipboard.
  3. #66623: Classifies context overflow in HTTP 200 error bodies and when no token count is given. This matters for gateways.
  4. #60074: Lets agents ask another session a question, which supports multi-session work.
  5. #65261: Adds agent widgets, which are interactive UI rendered natively by each client.
  6. #66516: Bumps google-auth-library to 10.6.1 to fix AWS Workload Identity Federation. It is flagged needs:compliance.
  7. #66517: Adds Ctrl+J to toggle the terminal pane. An earlier version broke the input.newline default, and this one addresses that.
  8. #66638: Keeps a script's Output row in place when its changes are grouped under full_codemode.
  9. #66538 (closed): Drops the Kimi system prompt override, so Kimi models use the default prompt.
  10. #66637 (closed): Fixes sticky file header layout, which was breaking e2e and component CI on dev.

5. Feature Request Trends

  • Subagent control: Foreground and blocking mode (#64073, #64096) and cancellation (#36423).
  • Skills UX: Autocomplete in the middle of a prompt (#40689) and skills in the slash list (#50638, #35341, both closed).
  • Plan mode parity with V1: #49879 (closed), and keeping the tab's model across plan/build switches (#54375).
  • Provider management GUI for custom providers and model lists (#33704).
  • Quota warnings before free-tier exhaustion (#42765).
  • Service control: An option to disable session auto-resume (#56032).
  • Multi-agent teams (#12259 is unrelated; see #12711, closed).

6. Developer Pain Points

  • Free tier and billing opacity: Limits are unclear, resets fail, and regional payments are declined (#59387, #52958, #66421).
  • V1→V2 migration fallout: Hidden sessions, wrong project assignment, and broken tool state (#49827, #50979, #51191, #66389).
  • Windows quality: Flashing console windows, unsafe shell quoting, and a plugin hook problem (#52266, #66449, #66299).
  • Runaway agents and token spend: Subagent loops and auto-resume after an unclean stop (#45442, #56032).
  • Cache and provider quirks: Prompt cache lost when reasoning effort changes on Copilot GPT-6 (#59868).
  • UI details: Lost scroll position on desktop (#55699), a question modal that blocks text (#37173), and a dropped double n in the TUI composer (#66557).
  • macOS network access: Local Network Privacy blocks LAN hosts, and users suggest a signed .app bundle (#58080).

item.content:encoded:
MCP Ecosystem Digest 2026-11-27

Issues: 2 | PRs: 0 | Projects covered: 7 | Generated: 2026-11-26 17:29 UTC

  • MCP Servers
  • MCP Registry (official)
  • Awesome MCP Servers
  • Docker MCP Registry
  • Claude Plugins (official)
  • Awesome Claude Code
  • Awesome Agent Skills

MCP Deep Dive

MCP Servers Project Digest — 2026-11-27

1. Today's Overview

Activity in modelcontextprotocol/servers was very low over the last 24 hours. Only 2 issues were updated, and both are open enhancement requests labeled v2. There were no PRs, no merges or closures, and no new releases. The repository looks quiet on the code-change side, with discussion centered on the v2 / "Modern (2026-07-28)" protocol era. Both issues have no comments, so maintainers have not yet engaged.

2. Releases

No new releases.

3. Project Progress

No PRs were merged or closed today, so there is no feature or fix progress to report.

4. Community Hot Topics

Neither issue has comments, and reactions are minimal. By engagement:

  • #5660 — "Heads-up before I publish: runtime test results for mcp-server-time, mcp-server-git and mcp-server-fetch" (👍 1, 0 comments). The author, sarooo43, maintains the MIT-licensed tool mcp-caretaker. They are giving the maintainers advance notice of runtime test results for several reference servers. The underlying need is third-party validation and coordinated disclosure: external tooling now tests reference servers, and its authors want a courtesy channel before publishing findings. The issue is filed under the everything server and the "Modern (2026-07-28)" era.
  • #5659 — "git: add public agent skill to guide agents to use mcp-server-git tools over shell git" (👍 0, 0 comments). The author, mstred, reports that agents with shell access often fall back to raw git CLI commands even when mcp-server-git is connected. The need is better agent steering toward MCP tools, for example through a shipped skill or guidance file.

5. Bugs & Stability

No bugs, crashes or regressions were reported today. No fix PRs exist.

Note: #5660 refers to runtime test results for mcp-server-time, mcp-server-git and mcp-server-fetch. The excerpt does not show whether these contain defects. Maintainers should read the full issue to check whether any findings are real bugs.

6. Feature Requests & Roadmap Signals

  • Agent skill for mcp-server-git (#5659): This is a lightweight, documentation-style change that does not touch server code. It fits the v2 label and would be cheap to adopt. It is a plausible candidate for a near-term docs or packaging update, though no maintainer has responded yet.
  • Coordinated testing and disclosure (#5660): This is not a feature request in the usual sense. It does suggest growing demand for a conformance or runtime-testing story across reference servers.

Neither item has a linked PR, so I wouldn't predict either one for the next release.

7. User Feedback Summary

  • Agents ignore available MCP tools in favor of familiar shell commands. This weakens the value of dedicated servers such as git, which can offer safer and more structured operations.
  • Third-party ecosystem tooling is starting to exercise the reference servers at runtime. That is a sign of maturity, and it raises the question of how maintainers want findings reported.
  • No satisfaction or dissatisfaction signals appear beyond these two items.

8. Backlog Watch

Both issues were created on 2026-11-26 and are less than a day old, so neither counts as long-unanswered. Both have zero comments and need a first maintainer triage:

  • #5660 needs a response on how the author should disclose findings. It also appears to be filed against the wrong server (everything) and may need re-labeling.
  • #5659 needs a decision on whether a skill or guidance file belongs in this repo.

Today's data contains no older backlog items, so a wider backlog review would need data from a longer time window.

Project health: Low activity today, with no regressions or releases. The v2 label shows the issue templates are being used, but the lack of PRs and maintainer replies in this window suggests triage latency is worth watching.

Cross-Ecosystem Comparison

Cross-Project Comparison Report, 2026-11-27

Scope: MCP Servers, MCP Registry, Awesome MCP Servers, Docker MCP Registry, Claude Plugins (official), Awesome Claude Code and Awesome Agent Skills. Data covers the last 24 hours only. Docker MCP Registry figures cover the top 20 of 50 updated PRs. The Awesome MCP Servers sample is also partial.

1. Ecosystem Overview

The MCP ecosystem is currently driven more by distribution and curation than by core protocol code. The reference repo is quiet. Most activity is in catalogs and lists (Awesome MCP Servers: 259 PRs, Docker MCP Registry: 50 PRs, Awesome Agent Skills: 11 PRs). These absorb vendor and community submissions faster than maintainers can review them. Security and trust is the main technical theme: tool poisoning, scan receipts and hook safety. The ecosystem is also becoming multi-host. Skills and plugins now target Claude Code, Codex CLI and DeepSeek, and remote or hosted MCP servers are growing. Review capacity is the main bottleneck.

2. Activity Comparison

Project Issues updated PRs updated Release Health (my assessment)
MCP Servers 2 (both open, 0 comments) 0 None Low activity. Triage latency is a risk.
MCP Registry 1 4 (3 Dependabot) None Stable. Security design work is unresolved.
Awesome MCP Servers 0 259 (247 open, 12 closed) None (n/a) High intake, with a growing queue (~4.6% closed).
Docker MCP Registry 0 50 (48 open, 2 closed) None High intake, with a review bottleneck.
Claude Plugins (official) 11 (6 closed) 4 None Moderate. Maintainers respond, but a blocking bug is open (#7223).
Awesome Claude Code 0 0 None No activity in 24h.
Awesome Agent Skills 0 11 (10 open, 1 closed) None Steady intake. No merges today.

Health ratings are qualitative judgments from one day of data, not measured scores.

3. MCP Servers' Position

  • Role: It is the reference implementation (git, fetch, time, everything). It is not a catalog. It sets conventions that the registries and lists index.
  • Advantages: It has canonical status and is now a target for third-party runtime testing (#5660, mcp-caretaker). It is also the only project here tied to the v2 / "Modern (2026-07-28)" protocol era.
  • Differences in approach: Peers handle submissions (PRs adding entries). This repo handles server code and protocol evolution, so its volume is naturally lower.
  • Community size: It is the smallest by volume today (2 issues, 0 PRs) against 259 PRs for Awesome MCP Servers and 50 for Docker. This reflects workflow differences, not necessarily a smaller community. A 24-hour window can't establish long-term size.
  • Gap: Neither open issue has a maintainer response. Peers such as Claude Plugins show faster issue handling.

4. Shared Technical Focus Areas

Need Projects Specifics
Security and trust MCP Registry, Awesome MCP Servers, Claude Plugins, MCP Servers Tool-signature fingerprinting (#82), security-scan receipts (#1404), read-only and confirmation modes, a hook-timeout and temp-file fix wave, third-party runtime testing (#5660)
Agent steering toward tools MCP Servers, Awesome Agent Skills Agents prefer shell git over mcp-server-git (#5659). Skills are the proposed fix.
Cross-host portability Claude Plugins, Awesome Agent Skills Codex hook-schema failures. Skills for Claude Code, Codex CLI and DeepSeek.
Remote and hosted servers Docker MCP Registry, Awesome MCP Servers Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.1, empty tools.json for remote servers, Glama listings
Persistent memory Awesome MCP Servers, Awesome Agent Skills Local-first memory servers and context-engineering skills
Review and triage automation Awesome MCP Servers, Docker MCP Registry, Awesome Agent Skills Auto-merge or auto-close rules, remote-server criteria, submission checklists
Windows reliability Claude Plugins Git Bash hangs, pyenv-win artifacts

5. Differentiation Analysis

  • MCP Servers: reference code for protocol implementers.
  • MCP Registry: official metadata layer (server.json, _meta extensions). It is moving toward an attestation layer.
  • Awesome MCP Servers: a broad human-curated index. It uses Glama as a quality gate.
  • Docker MCP Registry: a catalog of containerized and remote servers. It leans toward enterprise or runtime users and is increasingly remote-first.
  • Claude Plugins (official): shipped, versioned plugins with SHA-pinned marketplace entries and a validation CI. It has the most hands-on bug traffic.
  • Awesome Agent Skills: a skills-centric list. Entries are vertical and portable across agents.
  • Awesome Claude Code: no data today, so no comparison is possible.

6. Community Momentum & Maturity

  • High-intake, review-limited: Awesome MCP Servers, Docker MCP Registry, Awesome Agent Skills. Contributors are engaged, but closure rates and maintainer comments are low.
  • Active maintenance: Claude Plugins. It has six closures in a batch, automated SHA bumps and a quick response to security-guidance. A few older bugs remain (#3937 open for about 4.5 months).
  • Stabilizing or slow: MCP Registry. Dependabot handles routine work, while #82 (open since 2025-05) and #1404 (about five months) are waiting on decisions.
  • Quiet: MCP Servers and Awesome Claude Code. One day is too short to call either dormant.

7. Trend Signals

  1. Trust is becoming infrastructure. Fingerprints, scan receipts and read-only modes recur across repos. Developers should plan for attestation metadata in registries.
  2. Hosted MCP is rising. Remote servers with OAuth dominate Docker submissions. Design for streamable HTTP and dynamic auth, and expect tool lists that can't be enumerated statically.
  3. Agents don't reliably prefer MCP tools. Shell fallbacks are common. Ship skills or guidance files alongside servers.
  4. Portability is expected. Hook and skill formats have to work on Codex and other hosts. Validate against strict schemas.
  5. Resource hygiene matters. Hangs, orphaned processes and temp-file growth (8.96 GB) are real operational risks. Set timeouts and handle stdin-EOF shutdown.
  6. Discovery is saturating. With hundreds of open listing PRs, quality gates and automation (Glama, checklists) will matter more than another list.

Caveat: this is a single-day snapshot with partial samples. Treat the rankings as directional.

item.content:encoded:
AI Infrastructure Digest 2026-11-27

Generated: 2026-11-26 17:29 UTC | Projects covered: 2

  • Dify
  • LiteLLM

Cross-Project Comparison

Cross-Project Comparison: Dify vs LiteLLM (2026-11-27)

Coverage caveat: Only two digests were supplied: Dify (an application and workflow platform) and LiteLLM (an LLM gateway). There was no data for inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, Ollama) or fine-tuning frameworks (Unsloth). Sections 3, 4 and 5 therefore say what is absent. They don't infer activity for projects I haven't seen.

1. Ecosystem Overview

Both projects spent the day on correctness, not new capability. Dify's work was frontend error and cache plumbing plus a long list of validation bugs in Agent V2, the CLI and the SDK. LiteLLM's was billing accuracy, Prometheus identity and provider-translation bugs. Neither digest reports benchmark numbers, new model launches or new hardware backends. The pressure is at the integration layer, where agents, tool calls, thinking signatures and cost accounting cross provider boundaries. LiteLLM shipped a release (v1.108.18) and Dify did not.

2. Activity Comparison

Neither digest gives totals. These counts are the unique issues and PRs linked in each digest, so they are approximate.

Project Issues referenced PRs referenced Release status
Dify ~30 (about 20 closed, most from one reporter, Afloat16) ~18 (mostly open; a hyoban frontend stack of ~10) None in 24h; the latest version discussed is v1.20.0
LiteLLM ~19 (mixed open and closed, many older) ~8 (several fix PRs, one breaking) v1.108.18 shipped (changelog truncated in the data); LTS 1.108.19 queued in #54723
  • Dify: Issue volume is inflated by a batch report against main at f6c206b. That batch reads like a sweep, not organic user traffic.
  • LiteLLM: Most of the issues listed are older tickets, not new ones. Day-specific activity is concentrated in about five PRs (#54719, #54721, #54722, #54723, #54725).

3. Model Support Race

There is no meaningful race in these two digests.

  • Dify: Nothing on models or hardware. Its only adjacent change is Qdrant BM25 ranking for full-text search (#47354).
  • LiteLLM: It is the only one with model-catalog work.
    • PR #54721 adds openrouter/google/gemini-4-argon, -carbon and -neon to the cost map.
    • PR #51434 adds the ProxyStacks Relay provider as openai_like, with 21 models.
    • Issue #36285 asks for Vertex AI RAG Engine as a vector-store provider.
    • PR #43448 (open, risk:high) adds a Rust gateway.
  • Who is ahead: On model breadth, LiteLLM, by default. Engine-level architecture support (new model families, kernels, quantization formats) can't be assessed without the vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp or Ollama digests.

4. Performance Frontier

None of the optimization areas you listed (KV cache, batching, quantization, distributed serving, kernels) appears in these digests. The performance work visible here is at the control plane and concurrency level:

  • Event-loop and worker blocking:
    • Dify #47222: the API worker freezes during an agent LLM dispatch, stalling co-hosted SSE streams and delaying workflow_started by minutes. No fix PR is linked.
    • LiteLLM #54719: moves the JWT custom_validate hook off the event loop.
  • Lock contention: LiteLLM #47579: the Presidio guardrail holds a session lock across HTTP calls, which serializes analyzer and anonymizer calls per process. No fix PR is visible.
  • Streaming reliability: Dify #47277 (Redis Streams can miss events after an idle read, closed) and #47301 (open 5xx response bodies hold connections, closed).
  • Test infrastructure: Dify PR #47356 isolates SSRF retry sleeps after a merge-queue timeout.

No numbers were reported by either project, so none of this can be ranked quantitatively.

5. Layer Positioning

Project Layer Evidence today
Dify Application and agent platform, sitting above the model layer Workflow editor, Agent V2, MCP, HITL forms, tracing (Langfuse), RAG backends, CLI and SDKs
LiteLLM LLM gateway and proxy, between applications and providers Provider translation, cost and spend tracking, Prometheus metrics, guardrails (Presidio), JWT auth, MCP session limits
  • Overlap: Both handle MCP, tracing and observability, and credential fallback. Dify's #47256 (hosted-credit exhaustion bypasses the custom-credential fallback) is the kind of problem a gateway usually owns.
  • Gaps in this report: No serving-engine, local-runtime or training layer was supplied, so comparing those layers isn't possible here.

6. Trend Signals

  1. Cost accounting is a correctness problem.
    • Examples: LiteLLM #54722 (billing Anthropic refusals that Anthropic doesn't charge), #46499 (partial spend on mid-stream disconnects) and #46059 (lost watsonx streamed usage).
    • Reconcile gateway spend against provider invoices.
  2. Provider portability is leaky.
    • Thinking signatures and tool-call IDs don't transfer between providers (LiteLLM #54561, #38270, #48401).
    • Pin a conversation to one provider for now.
  3. Agent V2 is still maturing.
    • Dify v1.20.0 has open issues: dynamic MCP headers (#47224), Langfuse export dropping whole traces on spans over 1 MiB (#47327) and 502 binding_create_failed (#47355).
    • Prefer the legacy Agent or keep tool outputs small if you depend on these.
  4. Observability contracts are shifting.
    • LiteLLM's breaking Prometheus change (#54725) moves to a canonical deployment identity, so update dashboards and alerts first.
    • Dify is moving the UI to code-based error translation (#47331), so integrations should parse error codes, not message text.
  5. Isolation for streaming workloads. Dify's worker freeze (#47222) means SSE endpoints shouldn't share workers with agent dispatch until it is fixed.
  6. Security and supply chain. LiteLLM's LTS line carries the OpenSSL 3.5 backport via #54723, and its image verification uses cosign.

To make this a true infrastructure-layer comparison, re-run it with the vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, Ollama and Unsloth digests. Sections 3 and 4 would then have real content.

Per-Project Reports

Dify — langgenius/dify

Dify Digest — 2026-11-27

1. Today's Highlights

No release today. Activity centers on two things. The first is a large frontend stack from hyoban that centralizes request-error translation and automatic cache invalidation. The second is a batch of about 20 bug reports from Afloat16 against main at f6c206b. Most of those reports are already closed. On the stability side, the open reports are about Agent V2 in v1.20.0: dynamic MCP headers, Langfuse trace export, and Dify Agent 502 errors.

2. Releases & Breaking Changes

No releases in the last 24h.

Behavior changes in open PRs:

  • Request errors by code: A cataloged backend error code now shows its translated text instead of the backend's English message. PR #47331, PR #47332, and the per-domain migrations #47333, #47334, #47335, #47336.
  • Invalidation fallback: After every successful console write, the mutation's own domain is refreshed in the background. Per-domain cleanups follow. PR #47328, #47329, #47343, #47344.
  • Human Input (HITL) forms: New date and datetime field types across the v1 and v2 pipelines. PR #47348 fixes Issue #46911.
  • Swedish (sv-SE) locale: PR #46859, tracked in Issue #42448.

3. New Model & Hardware Support

Nothing on models or hardware backends today. Related backend changes:

  • PR #47354: Qdrant full-text search ranked with BM25. Today it is unranked.
  • Issue #47283 (closed): IRIS pool settings supplied as environment strings fail before numeric validation.

4. Performance & Optimization

No benchmarks with numbers today.

  • Issue #47222: The API worker process freezes for the whole duration of an agent LLM dispatch (inner API → plugin daemon). Co-hosted SSE streams stall, and workflow_started is delayed by minutes. This is the most significant latency problem reported today, and no fix PR is linked.
  • Issue #47277 (closed): Live Redis Streams subscriptions can miss events after an idle read, because $ keeps being passed to XREAD.
  • Issue #47271 (closed): Long but valid trace trees hit RecursionError during normalization.
  • Issue #47301 (closed): CLI device polling leaves 5xx response bodies open across retries, which holds connections.
  • PR #47356: Isolates SSRF retry sleeps in tests. A merge-queue run for #47177 timed out because of this.

5. Stability & Regressions

Ranked by severity.

Open

  1. #47222: Worker freeze during agent dispatch (see above). No fix PR.
  2. #47355: On v1.20.0, Dify Agent returns HTTP 502 binding_create_failed with an empty message. PR #47230 may be related. It reports job details on an empty binding setup error, but it doesn't clearly fix the 502. Treat the link as unconfirmed.
  3. #47256: DifyPreparedPollingLLM bypasses the HostedCreditFallbackModelInstance custom-credential fallback when hosted credits run out. No fix PR.
  4. #47327: In Agent V2, oversized spans over the hardcoded 1 MiB delivery limit stop the whole workflow trace from being exported to Langfuse. No fix PR.
  5. #47224: Dynamic MCP HTTP headers are not resolved in Agent V2 but work in legacy Agent (v1.20.0). No fix PR.
  6. #46861: Plugin provider lists report daemon failures as invalid input.
  7. PR #43241 (fix open): Required Number inputs reject 0 in workflow Test Run.
  8. PR #47177 (fix open): Reconnecting editor pages can leave stale collaboration sessions in the same workflow room.

Reported and closed today (all from Afloat16)

  • #47269: Archive uploads to KMS-encrypted S3 buckets fail after a successful PutObject.
  • #47284: Remote Nacos/Apollo JSON mapping settings fail DifyConfig validation.
  • #47265: Strict evaluation schema normalization rewrites literal JSON values.
  • #47281: A serialized chunked trigger request loses its body on replay.
  • #47309: Workflow publish depth validation misses longer paths after branches merge.
  • #47311: MCP workflow tools skip required input schema validation.
  • #47313: Required multi-select tool inputs bypass empty-selection validation.
  • #47315: Imported workflows lose saved node positions or keep missing coordinates.
  • #47323: Navigating to nested workflow nodes centers on parent-relative coordinates.
  • CLI: #47291 (JSON pointer escaping), #47293 (search skips composed and map-value schema descriptions), #47295 (slow_down handling violates RFC 8628), #47297 (repeated stdin references read an exhausted stream).
  • Node SDK: #47305 (binary bodies enumerated as JSON fields), #47317 (JSON metadata dropped for published pipeline runs).

The issue list doesn't show whether fixes for these closed issues have merged. Check the linked PRs before assuming main is clean.

6. What This Means for Application Developers

  • Agent V2 on v1.20.0 has gaps. Dynamic MCP headers don't resolve (#47224). Langfuse export drops whole traces when one span exceeds 1 MiB (#47327). Agent runs can fail with 502 (#47355). If you depend on any of these, stay on the legacy Agent or keep tool outputs small.
  • Co-hosting agents and SSE on one API worker is risky (#47222). Until a fix lands, isolate streaming endpoints from agent-dispatch workers.
  • Custom-credential fallback is unreliable when hosted credits run out (#47256). Don't rely on automatic failover for hosted-credit exhaustion.
  • Integrations that parse backend error text should switch to error codes. The UI is moving to code-based translation (#47331).
  • HITL forms may gain date and datetime inputs once #47348 merges.
  • Node SDK and CLI users: several input-handling bugs were reported and closed today (#47305, #47317, #47297). Watch the next release for fixes.
  • Contributor opportunity: the good first issue threads #45584 (use the SQLAlchemy engine), #45585 (reduce Mock(spec=...)), and #45166 (pass Session into properties) remain active. PR #46913 is progress on #45584.
LiteLLM — BerriAI/litellm

LiteLLM Digest — 2026-11-27

1. Today's Highlights

LiteLLM shipped v1.108.18. A 1.108.19 LTS bump is already queued in #54723, and it carries the OpenSSL 3.5 backport. Most of the day's activity was billing and cost-accounting correctness (Anthropic refusals, custom pricing on passthrough routes, interrupted streams) plus Prometheus deployment-metric fixes. Cross-provider translation bugs (Bedrock/Vertex thinking signatures, OpenRouter reasoning chunks, Gemini IDs leaking through /v1/responses) keep coming in.

2. Releases & Breaking Changes

  • v1.108.18: the release notes in the data are truncated, so the changelog isn't visible here. The only content shown is the cosign image-verification snippet (ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.108.18).
  • Next LTS, 1.108.19 (#54723, open): the daily LTS patch release on lts/1.108.x. It picks up the OpenSSL 3.5 backport (#54428). enterprise/ and litellm-proxy-extras/ are unchanged.
  • Breaking, pending: #54725 fix(prometheus)! moves deployment metrics to a single canonical deployment identity. The ! marks it as breaking. Dashboards and alerts keyed on alias-based series labels will likely need updating when it lands.
  • Related deprecation thread: #9753 covers the deprecation of the Prisma Python client. It is stale with 22 comments and still has no migration plan.

3. New Model & Hardware Support

  • #54721 (open) adds openrouter/google/gemini-4-argon, -carbon and -neon to the model cost map. Only gemini-4-hydrogen is listed today.
  • #51434 (open) adds the ProxyStacks Relay provider as an openai_like provider with a 21-model cost map.
  • #36285 is a feature request for Vertex AI RAG Engine as a vector-store provider.
  • #43448 (open, risk:high) adds a Rust gateway with UI, native MCP and shared route lifecycle.

4. Performance & Optimization

No concrete benchmark numbers were reported. Relevant items:

  • #54719 moves the JWT custom_validate hook off the event loop and awaits async validators. A slow validator currently blocks the whole worker, health checks included, which can get a healthy pod restarted.
  • #47579 reports that the Presidio guardrail holds a session lock across the HTTP request. This serializes all analyzer and anonymizer calls per process. It is open with no fix PR visible.
  • #43583 (closed) reported fire-and-forget audit-log tasks dropping records on worker shutdown.

5. Stability & Regressions

Ranked by severity:

  1. Billing and cost accuracy
    • #54722 is a fix PR. LiteLLM priced Anthropic refusals that Anthropic doesn't bill. One example was $0.12 for a refused 1h cache write. Refusals in the bio, frontier_llm and reasoning_extraction categories are still billed.
    • #54390 and #54389 (both closed) covered custom deployment pricing being ignored on the OpenAI passthrough route and in batch cost tracking.
    • #46499 (open) says a client disconnect mid-stream logs only partial spend, while Bedrock bills the full output.
    • #46059 (closed) says watsonx streamed usage was lost and replaced by a lower proxy estimate.
  2. Cross-provider and translation correctness
    • #54561 (open): Bedrock Converse rewrites tool root schemas, so signed thinking blocks fail with a 400 when a conversation moves to Vertex.
    • #38270 (open): /v1/responses leaks Gemini thought signatures and foreign function-call IDs to other providers.
    • #48401 (open): streaming drops OpenRouter chunks that carry only reasoning_details, such as Claude signatures.
    • #53716 (open): azure_ai models hit ContextWindowExceededError through OpenWebUI.
    • #47928 is a fix PR for multi-turn assistant history being dropped on /v1/responses.
    • #47046 (closed): Gemini context caching reordered the conversation and dropped system_instruction.
  3. Security, data and config
    • #47605 (closed): Presidio in logging_only mode masked responses returned to the client.
    • #54467 (closed): /team/update replaced metadata instead of merging it, silently dropping turn_off_message_logging.
    • #35383 (open): the MCP stateful session cap is bucketed by API key, so shared keys share one 100-session limit.
  4. Observability
    • #54725 is a fix PR for a deployment-state series stuck at 2 after recovery.
    • #38494 (closed): custom_prometheus_metadata_labels caused a label-count ValueError on cooldown.
    • #53040 (open): a request for Prometheus outcomes on routed fallback attempts.

6. What This Means for Application Developers

  • Cost tracking: If you use custom pricing, Anthropic refusals, interrupted streams or passthrough routes, reconcile LiteLLM spend against provider invoices. Several of these paths were wrong, and some fixes are only now landing.
  • Moving a conversation between providers (Bedrock and Vertex, or Gemini and other providers via /v1/responses): thinking signatures and tool-call IDs are not portable. Pin a conversation to one provider until #54561 and #38270 are resolved.
  • Ops: Plan for the Prometheus identity change in #54725 before upgrading. Use the 1.108.x LTS line if you want OpenSSL 3.5. If you run async JWT validators, #54719 removes the event-loop blocking risk.
  • Guardrails and MCP: Presidio throughput is serialized per process, and MCP session limits are per key. Both matter for high-concurrency or shared-key deployments.
  • trim_messages(): #54442 says it can split tool calls from their tool responses. Avoid it for agent histories for now.

item.content:encoded:
AI Open Source Trends 2026-11-27

Sources: GitHub Trending + GitHub Search API | Generated: 2026-11-26 17:29 UTC

AI Open Source Trends Report, 2026-11-27

Data caveat: Trending-list repos report total stars as 0, which means the total is missing, so I show "n/a" and use only the "+today" figure. Topic-search star counts look unreliable. A single-purpose repo such as cleanyourtv (a TV debloater) shows 61,173 stars, and several near-identical "Grok Bot alternative" repos show five-figure totals. I treat those totals as possibly inflated or botted and don't rank on them.

1. Finds

  • Tracer-Cloud/opensre is an open-source agent aimed at CI/CD reliability, meaning failing pipelines and flaky builds. It's for platform and SRE engineers who want an agent for on-call and pipeline triage rather than another coding assistant. It gained +325 today, a modest and credible number.
  • microsoft/TokenEconomizer does "experience-driven black-box cost control for coding agents". It appears to learn from past runs to cut token spend without modifying the agent. Teams paying large coding-agent bills should look at it. The description is thin, so check the README for benchmarks before trusting it.
  • aoci-spec/aoci-code is a Go MCP server and CLI that keeps a Git-versioned map of your code and database schema, which agents read before editing. It targets people who use Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or opencode on large or legacy repos and want persistent context instead of re-exploring every session.
  • EL4CTEO/fast-anything takes a narrower approach than whole-app rewrites. It profiles a Python, Node or Ruby app, ports only the hot functions to Rust with a coding agent, and checks that behavior stays the same. Anyone with a slow service they don't want to rewrite would find it practical. Its sibling erkamyaman/rust-anything does the whole-app version.
  • qybaihe/bla is a defensive MCP server and CLI that obfuscates JS/TS, Electron ASAR, WASM, native binaries and GGUF/Safetensors against AI reverse-engineering agents. It is a new category, anti-agent protection, and is aimed at vendors shipping client-side code or model weights. Its effectiveness is unproven.
  • yetone/magpie is a Go tool that pools several paid AI plans (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, GLM, Kimi) behind one endpoint and fails over when one hits its quota. It is useful if you juggle subscriptions, but check each provider's terms first, because sharing plan access may violate them.

Looks like hype or a thin shell:

  • Ebony-Vinyl/dsh-our-free-model promises unlimited free frontier models with no key. That claim should make you look closely at where traffic is routed and who pays for it.
  • google/elephant-goldfish-model has a vague description and an implausible star count.
  • The cluster of "Grok Bot alternative" repos (OpenMausBot, rakazo, AnyModelBot, OpenBot) reads like templated marketing.

2. Top Projects by Category

🔧 AI Infrastructure

Project Lang Stars (total / today) Summary
microsoft/TokenEconomizer Python 8,141 Black-box cost control for coding agents, driven by past run experience. It is the only cost-governance project here from a major vendor.
aoci-spec/aoci-code Go 3,062 A local-first MCP server that gives agents a persistent, versioned index of code and DB schema. It targets the repeated context-rebuilding problem across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and opencode.
EL4CTEO/fast-anything Rust 4,186 Profiles slow apps and ports only the hot paths to Rust, then verifies equivalent behavior. It is a pragmatic alternative to full rewrites.
openvinotoolkit/openvino C++ n/a (+176) Intel's toolkit for optimizing and deploying AI inference. It is established, and the steady daily gain suggests ongoing edge and CPU inference demand.
yetone/magpie Go 41,967 Pools multiple paid AI plans and fails over when one runs out. It appeals to multi-subscription users but carries terms-of-service risk.
INK-Q/agy-fast TypeScript 1,691 An MCP accelerator plugin for Google Antigravity that claims 34% fewer LLM turns and 31% less token quota. The numbers are self-reported.
firecrawl/firecrawl TypeScript n/a (+1,042) A single API to search, scrape and access 550+ data providers for agents. It is already well known, but it is the strongest mover in agent data plumbing today.
cursor/plugins TypeScript n/a (+268) Cursor's plugin specification plus official plugins. It signals that editor-side plugin standards are becoming formal.

🤖 AI Agents / Workflows

Project Lang Stars (total / today) Summary
elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter Python n/a (+1,600) A Claude Code skill bundle with 85 skills, 16 slash commands and 681 disclosed-report patterns across 24 vulnerability classes. It is the day's top gainer, and the same code is useful for authorized testing and for abuse, so use it only with authorization.
obra/superpowers Shell n/a (+853) An agentic skills framework and development methodology. It is already well known, and its continued climb shows skills-as-methodology is mainstream.
HKUDS/CLI-Anything Python n/a (+744) Aims to make any software agent-native through CLIs, with a hub at clianything.cc. The idea is to wrap existing GUI apps so agents can drive them.
Tracer-Cloud/opensre Python n/a (+325) An open-source agent for CI/CD reliability. It is a vertical, operations-focused agent rather than a coding assistant.
n8n-io/nod TypeScript 3,873 A personal agent with its own computer that works on real websites and asks before acting. It is notable because n8n, an established automation vendor, is behind it.
reason-machines/reason-network Rust 1,819 Lets a team's coding agents communicate with each other. It is an early example of cross-agent coordination.
autonomous-ai/openharness TypeScript 1,535 A command center for running multiple coding agents across multiple machines. It extends beyond code into CAD, circuits and music.
DIYgod/pinky Go 2,809 Lets MCP agents operate a real iPhone or Android phone with a human in the loop. It comes from a well-known open-source author.

📦 AI Applications

Project Lang Stars (total / today) Summary
zhouxiaoka/autoclip Python n/a (+770) A local-first open-source OpusClip alternative that turns long videos into short clips with subtitles, covers and captions. It also runs as an MCP server and has no subscription.
cathrynlavery/diagram-design HTML n/a (+951) A skill with 52 diagram types, output as self-contained HTML and SVG, for Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor and others. It is a niche but practical alternative to Mermaid output.
mvanhorn/last30days-skill Python n/a (+755) An agent skill that researches a topic across Reddit, X, YouTube, HN, Polymarket and the web, then writes a grounded summary. It is useful for fast research briefs.
mjmirza/app-store-compliance Shell n/a (+561) A playbook and pre-submission guard with 125 rejection patterns and 117 tracked regulatory deadlines, including the EU AI Act. It suits mobile teams that want to avoid review rejections.
openfilm/openfilm TypeScript 9,498 Turns a coding agent into a video agent, with editors to adjust the output. It is part of a wave of agent-driven video tools.
genspark-ai/genoffice TypeScript 12,989 An open-source office suite with a built-in agent and a CLI so Claude Code, Codex and Cursor can edit real .docx, .xlsx and .pptx files. Its main value is the file-level agent interface.
google-labs-code/stitch-skills TypeScript n/a (+308) Agent Skills built for the Stitch MCP server, compatible with Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Claude Code and Cursor. It shows Google adopting the Agent Skills open standard.

🧠 LLMs / Training

Project Lang Stars (total / today) Summary
jingyaogong/minimind Python n/a (+701) Trains a 64M-parameter LLM from scratch in about two hours. It is a good educational path through the whole pretraining pipeline on modest hardware.
Human-Agent-Society/reef Python 7,621 Infrastructure for continually self-improving agents. The concept is interesting, but check the README for evidence of real improvement.
bojieli/ai-infra-book Python 8,346 An open-source book (in Chinese) on quantitative analysis of LLM inference and training system design, with calculation tools and experiments. It is valuable as reference material.
modelscope/ms-cookbook HTML 547 A practical guide covering model selection, inference, fine-tuning, evaluation, RAG and agents. It is a good on-ramp, and the low star count suggests it is still undiscovered.

🔍 RAG / Knowledge

Project Lang Stars (total / today) Summary
Zleap-AI/SAG-Wiki Rust 1,698 A lightweight knowledge base for people and agents with fast indexing and precise retrieval. The Rust implementation targets low overhead.
crow-hq/llm-wiki-v2 Python 329 Turns documents into a readable Markdown wiki that answers with citations, and works with any provider including Ollama. It claims 63% fewer tokens, which is self-reported and worth verifying.
YOLOW92/pagesift Rust 314 A local-first ingestion engine with HTTP and browser capture, layout-aware PDF, Office and OCR parsing, and evidence-grounded context. It is aimed at the unglamorous but hard problem of document ingestion.
Dongbumlee/ontosmith Python 300 Builds governed knowledge graphs where each fact is traceable to its source evidence. It suits regulated or audit-heavy domains.
FengZhenfei/carrel Python 799 Ontology-augmented generation for agents. It is an early, small project exploring structure beyond plain vector retrieval.

3. Trend Signal Analysis

Skills are the dominant packaging format. Six of the 16 trending repos are agent skills or skill bundles: Claude-BugHunter, superpowers, diagram-design, last30days-skill, stitch-skills and app-store-compliance. The topic search shows the same pattern in agent-skills and claude-code. Compatibility lists now name Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Pi and Antigravity together, so Agent Skills is becoming a cross-vendor standard. Google's stitch-skills and Cursor's plugin spec are signs of vendor adoption.

New directions:

  • Agent-driven media creation. Video, film styles and animated explainers are produced by coding agents writing code instead of calling video models (openfilm, lemo-opuscar, video-talkcraft, stickman-video-director).
  • Agent cost and context governance. TokenEconomizer, agy-fast and aoci-code treat token spend and persistent codebase memory as products.
  • Anti-agent defense. bla is a rare defensive project against AI reverse-engineering.
  • Agents operating phones. pinky, Mika and esp32-iphone-agent let agents control real phones.
  • A "DeepSeek Harness" (dsh) plugin ecosystem. Several repos (dsh-TUI, dsh-Go, dsh-email, dsh-ppt, EAC-Desktop) build on it, though their star counts are unreliable.

Industry connection: Repeated mentions of Opus 5.5, Seedance, DeepSeek V4.1 and Kimi K3 suggest that stronger code-writing models are making "agent writes the artifact in code" practical. The "Grok Bot alternative" clones suggest a recent closed-product launch is being copied quickly.

Signal quality: Much of the topic-search list looks inflated or promotional. Weight the trending list more heavily.

4. Community Hot Spots

  • Skills and plugin standards (obra/superpowers, google-labs-code/stitch-skills, cursor/plugins): Write skills once and run them across agents. Watch for portability gaps.
  • Agent cost and context control (microsoft/TokenEconomizer, aoci-spec/aoci-code): Token spend and context reuse are now the practical bottleneck for coding-agent teams.
  • Vertical operations agents (Tracer-Cloud/opensre): CI/CD and SRE agents are more defensible than general coding assistants.
  • Making existing software agent-callable (HKUDS/CLI-Anything, firecrawl/firecrawl, genspark-ai/genoffice): CLIs, MCP servers and file-format tooling are becoming the interface layer.
  • Security on both sides of agents (elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter, qybaihe/bla): Offensive skill packs are trending alongside defenses against agent-based reverse engineering. Treat both with authorization and licensing in mind.

item.content:encoded:
Hacker News AI Community Digest 2026-11-27

Source: Hacker News | 30 stories | Generated: 2026-11-26 17:29 UTC

Hacker News AI Community Digest — 2026-11-27

1. Today's Highlights

Math breakthroughs and AI-lab economics dominate HN today. The matrix multiplication exponent paper (1,056 points) and the refutation of the polynomial Hirsch conjecture, both from OpenAI's math preprints, drew heavy attention. Alongside them, Anthropic trading below its $83 IPO price (796 comments) and OpenAI cutting GPT-6.2 usage limits fed a thread of cost and trust worries. GLM-5.4 and the "LLM agents work for their parent companies" essay also scored above 1,000. Overall mood: impressed by capability, wary of the business side and of vendor control.

2. Top News & Discussions

🔬 Models & Research

Title Score Comments Summary
The matrix multiplication exponent is nine fourths [pdf] · HN 1056 603 A claimed improvement to a long-standing open problem in theoretical computer science, published as an OpenAI preprint. The community is excited but skeptical, and wants independent verification and clarity on how much the AI contributed.
GLM-5.4: Toward generalized coding with our first loop transformer · HN 1180 386 Z.ai's first loop-transformer model, aimed at coding, is the top-scoring item in the feed. Readers are interested in the architecture and in how competitive it is with the closed frontier models.
The polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false [pdf] · HN 173 45 Another OpenAI math preprint, this one refuting a well-known conjecture in polytope theory. Discussion is brief and focuses on whether the result holds up.
GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities · HN 355 97 OpenAI says general-purpose models can design proteins without specialized training. Reactions mix interest in the science with concern about biosecurity and about vendor-reported claims.

🛠️ Tools & Engineering

Title Score Comments Summary
Bare Metal Qwen · HN 220 53 Runs Qwen inference on bare metal with no OS. HN readers like this kind of low-level hacking and treat it as a way to learn how inference works.
Porting Rockbox to an undocumented $9 Aliexpress 'YP3' MP3 Player with LLMs · HN 265 101 A practical case of LLMs helping with reverse engineering of undocumented hardware. The community sees it as a good example of AI assistance in hard, niche engineering.
PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches · HN 401 78 A small generative model for handwriting and sketches with a clear write-up. Readers like the approachable, hands-on style.
Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email · HN 93 107 Points out functional gaps in Google's official Workspace MCP servers. The thread is mostly frustration with immature agent tooling.

🏢 Industry News

Title Score Comments Summary
Anthropic breaks below $83 IPO price · HN 431 796 The most-discussed thread of the day, on the market's verdict on AI-lab valuations. Opinions split between a bubble correction and normal post-IPO volatility.
OpenAI cuts GPT-6.2 usage: Astra hits limits 40% faster, Sol 25% faster · HN 424 239 Users get less usage from the same plans. Many complain, and some read it as a sign that inference costs are biting.
OpenAI may be in cost control mode · HN 13 3 A short analysis tying the usage cuts to cost pressure. It drew little discussion on its own.
The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features · HN 553 465 Concerns about how AI features in Photoshop handle content and rights. The thread is strongly worried about creator control.

💬 Opinions & Debates

Title Score Comments Summary
LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you · HN 1022 412 Argues that agents serve their vendors' incentives first. It resonates with readers who worry about lock-in and hidden steering.
Ask HN: Anthropic is accusing my company of distilling. How can I prove I'm not? · HN 459 352 A founder describes the difficulty of disproving distillation accusations. The community is sympathetic and critical of opaque enforcement.
Rumors swirling that labs might have cracked Factoring in P · HN 502 376 An unverified rumor with major cryptographic implications. Most commenters are skeptical and ask for evidence.
Multiagent coding is the future · HN 75 76 A practitioner's case for multi-agent coding workflows. Opinions are mixed, with some reporting gains and others citing coordination costs.

3. Community Sentiment Signal

The most active topics by score and comments are the matrix-multiplication preprint (1,056/603), GLM-5.4 (1,180/386), the agents-serve-vendors essay (1,022/412) and the Anthropic IPO thread (431/796). Consensus is that AI-assisted math and open models like GLM are impressive. Controversy centers on three points: whether vendor-published results can be trusted without verification, who benefits when agents are controlled by their makers, and the economics behind rising prices and tighter limits (OpenAI cuts, Anthropic's stock). The factoring-in-P rumor shows how readily HN engages with unverified claims, though the thread is skeptical. I have no data from the previous cycle, so I can't say how the focus has shifted. This feed leans toward business and trust concerns, with a smaller share of developer-tool excitement.

4. Worth Deep Reading

  1. The matrix multiplication exponent is nine fourths: If it holds, this is a major theoretical result, and the 603-comment thread should show early expert scrutiny.
  2. LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you: It frames incentive and trust questions that matter for anyone building on vendor agents.
  3. Migrating Our Messages API to Rust: A first-hand engineering account from a large-scale AI API, useful for infrastructure teams even though it drew little discussion (30 points).

This digest is auto-generated by agents-radar.

item.content:encoded:
ArXiv AI Research Digest 2026-11-27

Source: ArXiv (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.LG) | 50 papers | Generated: 2026-11-26 17:29 UTC

ArXiv AI Research Digest — 2026-11-27

1. Today's Highlights

Today's submissions center on agent evaluation and reliability. Several papers show that benchmark and monitor design can distort conclusions. These include attack-policy selection for AI monitors, coding-agent over-editing, and routeability of LLM benchmarks. Looped and recurrent architectures get fresh scrutiny, with Mixture-of-Loops and a critical look at looped MoE gains. Efficiency work targets long-context speculative decoding on natively sparse models. A theoretical result shows tokenisation is not in APX. A provocative finding is that coding agents can out-reason video generation models on visual reasoning tasks.

2. Key Papers

🧠 Large Language Models

Paper Authors Summary
Tokenisation is not in APX Violeta Kastreva, Philip Whittington, Dennis Komm et al. Proves that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm finds a tokeniser within a constant factor of optimal. This explains why tokeniser training relies on heuristics and sets a theoretical limit on the field.
Mixture-of-Loops Transformer Lianghui Zhu, Shijie Wang, Xinggang Wang et al. Rethinks what is passed between loops in looped Transformers, aiming at a better expressivity-efficiency frontier. It addresses the main cost of parameter-sharing depth.
LoopTitan: What Does Parameter Revisit Buy a Mixture-of-Experts? Zichen Tian, Yudong Lu, Xuansheng Wu et al. Re-examines the large gains reported for looped MoE over standard MoE at matched parameters, FLOPs and KV cache. It matters for judging whether looping is a real architectural advance.
Repairing the Trustworthiness of Distilled Language Models Kumar Shubham, Devendra Vyas, Vidushi Agarwal et al. Targets trustworthiness regressions that distillation introduces even when task performance is preserved, and does so without the original distillation corpus. It is practical for deploying small student models safely.

🤖 Agents & Reasoning

Paper Authors Summary
Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators Charlie Griffin, Oliver Makins, Asa Cooper Stickland et al. Shows, using an ex-production OpenAI monitor, that the measured false negative rate of AI monitors depends strongly on which attack policy generates the test transcripts. This calls into question how safety monitors for agents are evaluated.
How Much Do Coding Agents Over-Edit, and Why? Aakash Goel, Benjamin Steenhoek, Yu Hu Introduces Delta Residue Attribution, which replays trajectories to separate needed from unneeded edits in agent patches. It moves past patch size as a proxy for over-editing.
Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models Dezhi Luo, Fengyuan Yu, Haotian Zhang et al. Finds that coding agents outperform video generation models on visual reasoning tasks. This challenges the idea that reasoning in the visual medium is inherently better.
When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL Haowen Hou, Yicheng Liu, Zhen Huang et al. Handles all-fail groups in group-based RLVR on long-horizon tasks, where group-relative methods get no reward gradient. It does this by splicing in learner-conditioned options instead of complete solutions from a stronger model.
Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems Lukas Aichberger, Adam Golinski, Arno Blaas et al. Addresses the scarcity of verifier-accepted traces on hard math problems under independent Monte Carlo sampling. It does so by generating diverse alternative reasoning traces.

🔧 Methods & Frameworks

Paper Authors Summary
DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity Hong Liu, Rui Cen, Junhan Shi et al. Lets drafters share the target model's sparsity instead of keeping their own context cache, for natively sparse models such as DeepSeek-V4. It speeds up decoding where it is slowest.
Routeability Before Routing: RAP and RouteabilityBench Yihang Lu, Denica Kjorvezir, Ana Gjorgjevikj et al. Proposes auditing whether a benchmark has enough prompt-level variation for LLM routing to make sense. It guards against routing studies built on benchmarks where model differences are too coarse to support them.
DRBench Pro Han Huang, Yuchen Yan, Xingyu Wu et al. Offers a knowledge-centric benchmark for professional deep research agents, scoring which research directions a report covers and how deeply. It fills a gap left by report-quality benchmarks.
Guidance as Variance Matching Ali Backour, Artem Lukoianov, Frank Permenter et al. Argues that diffusion guidance does not improve the posterior-mean prediction at practical scales, and offers a variance-matching account of what it does. It helps explain a widely used but poorly understood technique.

📊 Applications

Paper Authors Summary
TASK Memory Jinkun Zhao, Wenjun Wu Targets use-time memory hallucinations, where an agent retrieves the right memory but contradicts it or applies it to the wrong question. It uses activation steering and knowledge editing to fix this.
μ-Bench Qihao Lin, Guanxu Chen, Shuhang Zheng et al. Benchmarks voice agents completing interdependent requests from several users while respecting per-user authority and privacy. It covers a deployment setting that single-user evaluations miss.

3. Research Trend Signal

Three signals stand out. First, evaluation validity is under scrutiny: papers on monitor attack policies, routeability audits, and over-edit attribution all argue that standard metrics or proxies mislead. Second, looped and recurrent computation is drawing both new designs (Mixture-of-Loops) and skeptical re-evaluation (LoopTitan), which suggests the field is checking its claims at matched budgets. Third, agent training and inference are being adapted to new realities. Examples are RL for all-fail rollouts on long-horizon tasks, speculative decoding on natively sparse models, and memory-hallucination mitigation. Cross-modal work also asks whether code-driven agents beat generative video for reasoning. Taken together, the field is moving from building capabilities to measuring them rigorously.

4. Worth Deep Reading

  1. Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators: It is a case study on a production-derived monitor, and its methodological point applies to any agent-safety evaluation. Read it if you rely on red-team transcripts to estimate monitor performance.
  2. Solve Vision with Code: Its claim cuts against the "reason natively in the visual medium" narrative. The comparison between code agents and video models should shape how visual reasoning is benchmarked.
  3. Tokenisation is not in APX: It is a clean theoretical result with lasting relevance, since it justifies heuristic tokeniser design across several formulations.

item.content:encoded:
Hugging Face Trending Models Digest 2026-11-27

Source: Hugging Face Hub | 30 models | Generated: 2026-11-26 17:29 UTC

Hugging Face Trending Models Digest — 2026-11-27

Today's Highlights

Thinking Machines' Inkling-2-Mini dominates the board. The base model has 6,181 likes, and at least six community derivatives sit alongside it: GGUF builds, an uncensored variant, an abliterated variant and a quantized MoE build. Qwen3.8-27B is the most-liked text model at 21,834 likes and 6.0M downloads, and its quantized and fine-tuned offshoots also trend. Lightricks' LTX-2.5 leads in video generation (13,525 likes, 3.0M downloads). Chinese labs (Tencent, Baidu, inclusionAI, SenseTime) and Aleph-Alpha also released new MoE and reasoning models.

Trending Models

🧠 Language Models

Model Author Likes Downloads Summary
thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini thinkingmachines 6,181 96,527 A multimodal image-text-to-text conversational model built on the inkling2_loop architecture. It is the origin of the day's largest derivative wave.
Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B Qwen 21,834 6,047,011 A 27B multimodal chat model from the Qwen family. It has the most likes and downloads of any text model on the list.
inclusionAI/Ling-3.2-air inclusionAI 246 1,467 An MIT-licensed vision-language MoE (bailing_moe_v3_vl) that ships eval results. The permissive license makes it easy to adopt.
inclusionAI/LingSante-3.1-flash inclusionAI 200 1,487 A hybrid-architecture (bailing_hybrid) text-generation model with custom code. It is a "flash" tier aimed at low-latency use.
Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1.1 Aleph-Alpha 168 837 A reasoning-focused MoE that runs on vLLM. It is a rare European entry on the list.
tencent/Hy4-flash tencent 721 10,479 A Hunyuan v4 "flash" multimodal model in Transformers format. It has the most likes among the new Chinese-lab releases.
baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Preview baidu 321 1,193 A preview of the ERNIE 5.5 MoE line in its fast tier. It signals Baidu's continued open-weight releases.
KRAFTON/Raon-1-mini KRAFTON 136 264 A small text-generation model from the game publisher KRAFTON. It is an uncommon entry from the gaming industry.
MemTensor/MemT-1.0-Pro MemTensor 135 806 A Nemotron-H-based text model with custom code, apparently aimed at memory-centric use. It adds to the hybrid Mamba-style architecture trend.
sensenova/SenseNova-Loop-9B sensenova 757 3,268 A 9B multimodal model using a "loop" architecture. It is compact enough for local use.

🎨 Multimodal & Generation

Model Author Likes Downloads Summary
Lightricks/LTX-2.5 Lightricks 13,525 3,041,405 An open video model covering image-to-video, text-to-video and video-to-video. It has the highest like count outside the LLM category.
inworld/voice-isolator inworld 935 15,244 An audio-to-audio model for speech denoising and voice isolation. It is a practical tool for audio cleanup.
higurashi-ai/Haru-4B higurashi-ai 1,041 10,026 A 4B full-duplex speech-to-speech model. It stands out because it can listen and speak at the same time.
nvidia/Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B nvidia 237 218 A 30B-total, 3B-active MoE text-to-image model built on the Nemotron-H backbone. It shows NVIDIA moving into image generation.
sand-ai/MAGI-2-preview sand-ai 258 0 A preview of a model that generates video with audio from text or images. It has no downloads yet, so it is trending on interest alone.
Lakonik/pi-H3 Lakonik 310 73,578 A distilled flow-matching model for joint audio-video generation. Its 73,578 downloads suggest quick uptake.

🔧 Specialized Models

Model Author Likes Downloads Summary
apple/DepthPro2 apple 1,273 0 A metric monocular depth estimator that also handles video depth. It is Apple's follow-up to Depth Pro.
facebook/sam-3d-body-dinov3 facebook 2,048 21,394 A 3D human mesh recovery and pose estimation model with a DINOv3 backbone. It extends the SAM family into 3D.
llamaindex/OCRia-nano-1 llamaindex 256 126 A small ONNX OCR model that converts PDFs to Markdown. It is designed for lightweight document parsing.
llamaindex/OCRia-1 llamaindex 110 419 A larger Qwen3.5-based OCR and document-to-text model. It is the full-size counterpart of OCRia-nano-1.

📦 Fine-tunes & Quantizations

Model Author Likes Downloads Summary
unsloth/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF unsloth 1,441 2,445,633 The Unsloth GGUF build of the Inkling-2-Mini MoE. Its 2.4M downloads are about 25 times the base model's.
AtomicChat/Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-GGUF AtomicChat 887 762,491 An uncensored LoRA-based GGUF variant of Inkling-2-Mini for llama.cpp. It draws heavy download interest.
orcarouter/Inkling-2-Mini-abliterated-GGUF orcarouter 249 12,157 An abliterated (refusal-removed) GGUF of Inkling-2-Mini for local use. It is another example of the quick uncensoring cycle.
strata-engine/Inkling-2-Mini-Strata strata-engine 192 2,965 A quantized MoE build of Inkling-2-Mini using the Strata engine. It is an alternative to GGUF-based compression.
prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2.5-27B-GGUF prism-ml 470 59,366 A 2-bit ternary GGUF of a 27B model for llama.cpp. It pushes extreme compression.
nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF nari-labs 181 14,337 A quantized Qwen3.8-27B tuned for coding-agent use. It targets local agentic coding.
harness-hub/Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted harness-hub 1,131 3,844 A PEFT adapter trained with async GRPO to fit the pi agent harness. Its 1,131 likes are high for so few downloads.
DavidAU/Qwen3.8-27B-TURBO-Fable-Cold-Fusion-735-882-Heretic-Uncensored-NEO-CODER-MAX-MTP-GGUF DavidAU 4,397 1,873,950 A merged, uncensored coding-oriented Qwen3.8-27B GGUF with multi-token prediction. It is the most-liked Qwen community fine-tune.
SulphurAI/Sulphur-3 SulphurAI 1,182 189,735 A fine-tune of MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3 under a custom license. It shows that MiniMax-H3 is attracting derivatives.
Sentinel7/h3 Sentinel7 2,092 0 An unlabeled, not-for-all-audiences repo with no downloads. Its 2,092 likes with zero downloads suggest its ranking may not reflect real usage.

Ecosystem Signal

Two families dominate. Inkling-2-Mini has produced at least five community variants in a few days, covering GGUF, uncensored, abliterated and quantized-MoE builds. Qwen3.8-27B is the other, with a large base model plus coding, agent-RL and merged derivatives. Fine-tuning is shifting toward agent harnesses (pi-adapted, NariQ coding agent) and away from plain chat tuning.

Open weights remain the norm. Chinese labs released MoE "flash" tiers, and Aleph-Alpha and NVIDIA released open models of their own. On quantization, ternary 2-bit GGUF and engine-specific formats (Strata) are being tested alongside standard GGUF. Uncensoring happens within days of a release. Some likes-to-downloads ratios, such as Sentinel7/h3 and MAGI-2-preview, point to hype or ranking noise. Treat them cautiously.

Worth Exploring

  1. Lightricks/LTX-2.5 — It is an open video model with 3M downloads and a broad set of modes (text, image and video to video). Try it as a local alternative to closed video APIs.
  2. harness-hub/Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted — It is a study case in RL-adapting an open model to a specific agent harness using async GRPO. The PEFT adapter is lightweight to test.
  3. higurashi-ai/Haru-4B — A small full-duplex speech-to-speech model is a good way to explore real-time voice agents without a large GPU.
